e.etymology: From Old English Aelfwine, made up of aelf, elf, and wine, friend.
namesakes: Alvin (leader of Alvin and the Chipmunks)

assoc.t: Alvin of Alvin and the Chipmunks

e.note: Expect the Chipmunks' shouted ALVIN! to follow the name around.

e.etymology: A short form of Germanic names ending in -lind, tender or soft, such as Sieglinde. English speakers later linked it with Spanish linda, pretty. It was the top US girls' name from 1947 to 1952.
namesakes: Linda Hamilton (Sarah Connor in The Terminator)
e.note: Strongly tied to women born in the 1940s and 50s; linda also means pretty in Spanish and Portuguese.

e.etymology: The English word liberty, from Latin libertas, freedom, used as a name. US use jumped around the 1976 Bicentennial and again after 2001.

assoc.t: the Statue of Liberty and the Liberty Bell
Liberty Mutual insurance and its Liberty, Liberty jingle

e.etymology: A medieval variant of Helena used in Finland, Sweden and Latvia, equivalent to Ellen and Elin. Helen comes from Greek Helene, often linked to a word for torch.
From an English surname, probably from a place name ending in leah, a woodland clearing. As a first name it follows Ainsley, Kinsley and Tinsley.
A modern American coinage joining the word lake with the -lyn ending, in the pattern of Brooklyn and Oaklyn.
From an English surname, Middle English Neil or Nell plus -son. As a first name it began as a tribute to Admiral Lord Nelson, the victor of Trafalgar.
namesakes: Nelson Mandela (South African president and anti-apartheid leader)

assoc.t: Nelson Mandela, South African president
nelson, a wrestling hold (full nelson, half nelson)

e.etymology: From the English surname and place name Waverley in Surrey, possibly Old English waefre, wavering, plus leah, clearing. Walter Scott's 1814 novel Waverley spread the name.

assoc.t: Wizards of Waverly Place, the Disney Channel series

e.etymology: From German Kaiser, emperor, from Latin Caesar; also a German surname. As a first name it is a recent American title name in the line of King and Prince.

assoc.t: Kaiser Permanente, the health care system
the Kaiser, title of Germany's emperors, notably Wilhelm II
kaiser roll, the crusty sandwich bun

e.note: Kaiser is the title of Germany's emperors, tied to Wilhelm II of World War I; many Americans also know it as Kaiser Permanente health care.

e.etymology: A short form of Wesley or Weston, English place names built on Old English west; Wesley adds leah, a clearing or meadow.
A modern spelling of Kinsley, an English surname from a Yorkshire place name meaning the clearing of Cyne, an Old English name built on cyne, royal.
From Arabic, where two names share this spelling: zahir, shining or radiant, from zahara, to shine, and zahir, evident or manifest, one of the names of God in Islam.
From Dakota winuna, firstborn daughter, a birth-order term that English speakers adopted as a personal name.
namesakes: Winona Ryder (actress in Beetlejuice and Stranger Things)

assoc.t: actress Winona Ryder
Winona, Minnesota

e.etymology: From an English surname, a worn-down form of the Norfolk place name Cawston; the surname can also be Italian, from a Venetian word for house. A modern first name in the Mason and Jason pattern.

e.meaning: woodland clearing of the Hrype tribe
e.etymology: From an English surname and place name: the Old English tribal name Hrype plus leah, a woodland clearing.

assoc.t: Ellen Ripley, Sigourney Weaver's hero of the Alien films
Ripley's Believe It or Not!
Tom Ripley, the con man of The Talented Mr. Ripley

e.etymology: A respelling of the English word chosen, picked out or favored, a name with Biblical overtones. Chozen is also Daniel's rival in The Karate Kid Part II and Cobra Kai.

assoc.t: sounds like the English word chosen
Chozen of The Karate Kid Part II and Cobra Kai

e.etymology: A phonetic respelling of Naomi, from Hebrew No'omi, pleasantness; in the Bible, the mother-in-law of Ruth. The spelling fixes the pronunciation as ny-OH-mee.
The Spanish variant of Alfonso, a Visigothic name usually read as adal, noble, plus funs, ready. Alonso Quijano is the real name of Cervantes's Don Quixote.
From Late Latin Seraphina, the name of early martyrs, from the Biblical seraphim, the six-winged angels whose Hebrew name means burning ones.
From a Scottish surname and place name, Gaelic dubh, dark, plus glais, stream. The Douglases were among Scotland's most powerful noble families.
namesakes: Douglas Adams (author of The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy)

assoc.t: Douglas fir, the evergreen timber and Christmas tree

e.etymology: From Old Norse Bjorn, from the word for bear; written Björn in Swedish and Icelandic and Bjørn in Danish and Norwegian.
namesakes: Bjorn Ironside (Viking hero of the series Vikings)

assoc.t: BabyBjörn, the baby carrier and bouncer brand
Bjorn Ironside of the TV series Vikings

e.etymology: From Italian Marianna, a form of Marianne and Mariana that goes back to Mariamne, an old Greek form of Miriam; it is also read as a blend of Maria and Anna.
A spelling of Stormy, from the English word. Stormi Webster, the daughter of Kylie Jenner and Travis Scott born in 2018, made this spelling familiar.
namesakes: Stormi Webster (daughter of Kylie Jenner and Travis Scott)

assoc.t: Stormi Webster, daughter of Kylie Jenner and Travis Scott
sounds like Stormy, as in adult-film actress Stormy Daniels

e.etymology: First recorded for a fourth-century Spanish noblewoman; its origin is obscure, perhaps the Greek island of Thera. Saint Teresa of Ávila and Mother Teresa carried it around the world.
namesakes: Mother Teresa (Nobel Peace Prize-winning nun and saint)
Teresa of Ávila (Spanish saint and mystic)
Teresa Giudice (Real Housewives of New Jersey star)

assoc.t: Mother Teresa, the Calcutta nun and saint

e.etymology: A spelling of Maisie, a Scottish pet form of Margaret, from Gaelic Mairead plus -sie. Margaret comes from Greek margarites, pearl.

assoc.t: Maisy Mouse of Lucy Cousins's picture books and TV show

e.etymology: A respelling of Cassidy, from the Irish surname O Caiside, descendant of Caiside, a byname from cas, curly-haired.

e.meaning: dahlia flower (Spanish); branch or vine (Hebrew, Arabic)
e.etymology: Several names meet here: Spanish dalia, the dahlia flower; Arabic daliya, grapevine; Hebrew daliyah, a hanging branch; and Lithuanian Dalia, a goddess of fate.
From French jolie, pretty. It is not a traditional given name in France; Americans took it up, helped by the fame of actress Angelina Jolie.

assoc.t: actress Angelina Jolie

e.etymology: The Italian and Spanish form of Frank, at first a member of the Germanic Franks, a tribal name that came to mean free. It is also short for Francesco and Francisco.
namesakes: Franco Harris (Hall of Fame Pittsburgh Steelers running back)

assoc.t: Francisco Franco, Spain's dictator from 1939 to 1975

e.note: In Spain the bare name recalls the dictator Francisco Franco.

e.meaning: son of the right hand (from Benjamin)
e.etymology: A short form of Benjamin, Hebrew for son of the right hand, and less often of Benedict. Ben is itself the Hebrew word for son.

assoc.t: Big Ben, the London clock tower
Ben & Jerry's ice cream
Ben's Original rice, formerly Uncle Ben's

e.etymology: A variant spelling of Hadley, an English surname from place names built on Old English haeth, heather, and leah, clearing.
An American coinage that reads as the word lake with an -en ending. It first drew notice through the character Laken Lockridge on the 1980s soap opera Santa Barbara.

assoc.t: Laken Riley, student killed in 2024; the Laken Riley Act

e.note: Widely known from Laken Riley, the Georgia nursing student killed in 2024, and the federal law named for her.
